content: Peanut allergy, also known as groundnut hypersensitivity, is a specific type of food allergy that is distinct from other nut allergies. It involves an immune system overreaction to dietary substances derived from peanuts, which can lead to severe physical symptoms in affected individuals. The prevalence of peanut allergy is approximately 1% among both adults and children, though studies suggest it is becoming more common in children. Approximately 25% of children with a peanut allergy eventually outgrow it. Management typically involves strict avoidance of peanuts and foods that may be contaminated with peanut particles, oils, or derivatives. The most severe cases of peanut allergy can result in anaphylaxis, a life-threatening condition requiring immediate administration of epinephrine. In 2007, the Centers for Disease Control reported 12 to 20 deaths from food allergies, with other sources estimating around 125 deaths annually in the United States. Peanuts are the leading cause of fatal allergic reactions. Several notable deaths from peanut allergy occurred in 2008, including: Andrew Michael Smith, an 8-year-old, who died in February after accidental exposure to peanut allergens at home. Carol Kiener, aged 66, who died in March following a severe allergic reaction to peanuts. Paul Anthony Thurston, aged 30, who died in April after being served a peanut butter sandwich in jail. Daniel Sargent, aged 30, who died in July after consuming a cookie containing peanut butter at a party. Brian Hom II, aged 18, who died in July after eating a dessert with trace amounts of peanuts at a resort in Cabo San Lucas. Dexter Skinner, aged 16, who died in July after eating a chocolate bar. The 2005 death of Christina Desforges, initially attributed to peanut exposure via a kiss from her boyfriend who had eaten a peanut butter snack, was later determined to be caused by asthma-related respiratory failure triggered by tobacco smoke at a party. Research by Jennifer Maloney indicates that peanut allergens typically clear from saliva within about an hour. Symptoms of peanut allergy are mediated by Immunoglobulin E (IgE) and other anaphylatoxins, which trigger the release of histamine and other mediators from mast cells. This process, known as degranulation, can lead to vasodilation of arterioles and bronchoconstriction in the lungs (bronchospasm). Symptoms may include: Vomiting Diarrhea Urticaria (hives) Angioedema (swelling of the lips, face, throat, and skin) Acute abdominal pain Exacerbation of atopic eczema Asthma Anaphylactic shock The British Dietetic Association warns that untreated anaphylactic shock can result in death due to airway obstruction (bronchospasm), hypotension, or heart failure. Symptoms typically occur within minutes to hours of peanut ingestion and may begin with sneezing and tingling sensations on the lips, tongue, and throat, followed by pallor, malaise, warmth, and lightheadedness. Severe reactions can recur after an apparent resolution within 1 to 6 hours. Asthmatics with peanut sensitivity are at higher risk of life-threatening reactions. Treatment for peanut allergy is evolving. Experts at Duke University Medical Center anticipate that immunotherapy for peanut allergies may become available within five years. This treatment aims to modify the immune response to peanuts, shifting it from an allergic to a non-allergic reaction. This development offers hope to affected individuals and their families, as the prevalence of peanut allergy has doubled between 1997 and 2002, now affecting about 1% of children. Prevention remains critical, with avoidance being the primary strategy. Individuals should carefully read labels on foods, medications, cosmetics, creams, and ointments. A history of allergic reactions after consuming peanuts strongly suggests an allergy. While promising drugs to counteract peanut allergies are under development, legal challenges have delayed their availability. In 2007, Dr. Mohamed Ahmedna of North Carolina Agricultural & Technical State University announced a process to create allergen-free peanuts. Initial testing demonstrated 100% inactivation of peanut allergens in whole roasted kernels, with no reactions observed in serum from severely allergic individuals. Food companies have expressed interest in licensing this process, which reportedly does not compromise the taste or quality of peanuts and may even facilitate easier processing for use in food products.
